title: Designing for other people
summary: A workbook other people fill in is a small product. Give it one place to type, labels that say the unit, rules kept in cells, and checks that tell the user what’s missing.
objectives: Separate inputs, calculations and outputs, and colour-code them so users know where to type.
Put units in labels and rules in cells, never inside formulas.
Flag missing fields with IF and COUNTBLANK, and show a status line.
Test a form the way a user will, including wrong entries.

p: When you build a workbook for yourself, you know where everything is. When other people fill it in, they don’t, and they will type in the wrong place.
Design for the person in a hurry, on a small laptop, on a Monday morning.
Every rule you add now saves a phone call later.
This module builds Rakshak’s purchase request form.
In real life: used to get purchase requests as emails with half the details missing. He spent an hour a day chasing quantities and dates.

p: Keep the cells people type in together, the working in one place, and the answers where they’ll be read. Colour tells users which is which.
Green: type here. Yellow: worked out, don’t touch.
Inputs run down one column, in the order people think of them.
Results sit below the inputs, so they read top to bottom.
In real life: said the new form was the first one nobody had asked her how to fill in.

p: A label should answer the question the user would otherwise ask. Put the unit in the label, so the cell can hold a plain number.
Dates: say which date (“Needed by”, not “Date”).
Money: say the currency and whether GST is included.
Short notes in grey italic beside tricky inputs.
In real life: typed “1,200 pcs” into a quantity cell. The total showed #VALUE! and the request sat unapproved for two days.

bad.title: Unclear
bad.text: “Qty” (pairs? boxes?) and a cell holding “1200 pairs”: text, so the order value shows #VALUE!

good.title: Clear
good.text: “Quantity (pairs)” and a cell holding 1200: a number, so the formulas work

check.q: Why put the unit in the label instead of the cell?
options: So the cell holds a plain number that formulas can use
check.explain: “1200 pairs” is text; 1200 is a number.

p: Beside each input, a formula says “Required” while the cell is empty. One status line counts what’s still missing.
`=IF(B3="","Required","")` fills down beside the inputs.
`COUNTBLANK(B3:B10)` counts the empty ones.
Join text and numbers with &.
In real life: now gets requests that say “Ready to send” at the bottom. If they don’t, he sends them straight back.

p: The director approves orders above ₹50,000. Put the 50,000 in a cell and point the formula at it, so changing the rule doesn’t mean changing formulas.
A rule people can see is a rule people can check.
Label the rule cell and colour it as an input.
Later lessons lock it, so only Farah can change it.
In real life: raised the approval limit from ₹25,000 to ₹50,000 last year. Three old forms still used ₹25,000 for months.

bad.title: Hidden in a formula
bad.text: `=IF(B12>50000,"Director","Manager")`: when the limit changes, someone has to find every formula

good.title: Kept in a cell
good.text: `=IF(B12>$E$4,"Director","Manager")`: change E4 and every formula follows

p: Before you send a form out, try to break it: leave cells empty, type text where numbers go, enter a date in the past.
Ask a colleague to fill it in while you watch, without helping.
Every question they ask is a label to improve.
Lesson 1.2 adds rules so wrong entries can’t get in at all.
In real life: tests every new form on the newest person in the office. “If Priya can fill it in on her first day, it works.”

frames.say: The inputs run down column B in green; the rule (the approval limit) sits in E4.
In **C3**: `=IF(B3="","Required","")`, filled down to C10. The supplier is missing.
Order value `=B8*B9` is ₹54,000; above the ₹50,000 limit, so `=IF(B12>$E$4,"Director","Manager")` says Director.
The status line counts the empty inputs. Type the supplier, and it says **Ready to send**.

lab.intro: Rakshak’s purchase request form has its inputs in **B3:B10** and the approval limit in **E4**. Add the checks and the results.

cells.A2: Type in the green cells only. The yellow cells work themselves out.

tasks.prompt: In **C3:C10**, show **Required** beside any input that is empty, and nothing beside the others.

mistakes.msg: Show nothing for a filled cell: the last part of IF is "", two double quotes.
Point at the input in the same row (B3), without $ signs, so it moves as you fill down.

tasks.prompt: In **B12**, the **order value**: quantity × unit price.
In **B13**, who approves: **Director** if the order value is above the limit in E4, otherwise **Manager**.

expect.regexMsg: Point at the rule in E4 instead of typing 50000, so the form follows when the limit changes.

mistakes.msg: Point at the rule in E4 instead of typing 50000, so the form follows when the limit changes.

tasks.prompt: In **B14**, the **days until needed**: from the request date to the needed-by date.
In **B15**, the status: **Ready to send** if none of B3:B10 is empty, otherwise **Missing 1 field(s)** (with the number of empty inputs).
hints: IF that count is 0, “Ready to send”; otherwise join “Missing ”, the count and “ field(s)” with &.

expect.regexMsg: Join the count into the message with &: "Missing "&COUNTBLANK(B3:B10)&" field(s)".

tasks.prompt: Fill in the missing input: the supplier is **Shree Polymers**.
Someone types **1,200 pcs** into B8 instead of 1200. What does the order value in B12 show?
tasks.explain: “1,200 pcs” is text, and text times a number gives #VALUE!. That’s why the unit belongs in the label, and Lesson 1.2 adds a rule that only accepts whole numbers.

why.2: Excel doesn’t treat the text as zero in multiplication.
why.3: The formula multiplies, it doesn’t copy.

options: When the rule changes you change one cell, and people can see the rule

quiz.q: What do the colours on Rakshak’s form mean?

points: Design for other people: **one place to type**, coloured, with **units in the labels**.
Keep **rules in cells** (`=IF(B12>$E$4,…)`), never typed into formulas.
Flag gaps with `=IF(B3="","Required","")` and a **COUNTBLANK** status line; test the form like a user.
